# Introduction

## Project Goals

Every hurricane season, thousands of homeowners in the southeastern United States file a flood insurance claim. Most of them are insured by the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP), the public scheme run by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). For an insurer, the first question is simple to ask and hard to answer: how many claims should we expect next year, and where? This expected number of claims per insured home, the claim frequency, drives the price of a policy and the reserves a portfolio needs.

Insurers have long answered this question with generalized linear models (GLMs), which are transparent and easy to explain. Machine learning methods such as gradient boosting promise better predictions by finding patterns that a GLM does not look for. Our project tests this promise on real flood data. We compare LightGBM, a gradient boosting method, with two classical count models, a Poisson GLM and a negative binomial GLM, on the claims and policies that FEMA publishes through its OpenFEMA platform.

We study FEMA Region 4, the eight states of the Southeast (Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina and Tennessee), from the coast of Florida to the hills of Kentucky. The models learn from 2010 to 2019 and are tested on 2020 to 2024, the way an insurer would use past years to predict future ones.

### Adjustments to the Proposal

- **From the whole United States to Region 4.** The national files hold 2,725,989 claims and 74,739,461 policy records, too heavy to process and share comfortably. Region 4 (787,274 claims and 31,463,858 policy records) remains large and varied, with coastal and inland states.
- **Training starts in 2010 instead of 2009**, because the policy records start during 2009 and that year is incomplete.
- **A claim counts when it is paid.** We count claims with a payment for building damage; counting all claims is kept as a check.
- **A county-level table for this update.** The final analysis will be at the level of the census tract, a neighborhood of a few thousand people. Building that table requires the raw files and is still in progress, so this update works with the same kind of table at the level of the county and flood zone (@sec-ds-clean).

## Research Questions

- **RQ1.** Does LightGBM predict flood claim frequency better than a Poisson GLM and a negative binomial GLM? The question is whether the extra flexibility of boosting improves predictions on years it has never seen, enough to give up the transparency of a GLM.
- **RQ2.** Does the answer hold both for Florida and for the other seven states? Florida holds about 71% of the policies, so a single overall score would mostly describe Florida.

We expect that:

- **H1.** LightGBM predicts better than both GLMs, because flood risk likely depends on combinations of factors, such as flood zone and location, that a simple GLM does not capture.
- **H2.** The two GLMs give similar predictions on average; the negative binomial model mainly describes the uncertainty better.
- **H3.** All models predict too few claims in the hurricane years of the test period, because nothing in the data tells them in advance which year a hurricane will strike.

## Related Work

@kousky2017flood describe more than one million NFIP claims from 1978 to 2012 and show how concentrated flood losses are in time and space. We use the same program, but we count claims per area and year, which also requires the policies to know how many homes were insured. GLMs, introduced by @nelder1972glm, are the standard tool for claim counts: a Poisson or negative binomial distribution, and an adjustment for the number of insured homes. @henckaerts2021boosting build full insurance tariffs with tree-based methods and find that boosted trees beat a GLM benchmark. LightGBM [@ke2017lightgbm] is a fast implementation of boosted trees that suits a dataset of our size. Our project asks whether this advantage carries over to flood claims, where the data are anonymized and the test years contain some of the most destructive hurricanes on record.
